examples.label: Lecture grammar
examples.purpose: Small grammar with no conflicts in any method; the automaton is easy to follow.

examples.label: Comma-separated lists
examples.purpose: Left-recursive list rules, which LR parsers handle naturally.

examples.label: Simple declarations
examples.purpose: A practical declaration grammar with an optional array suffix.

examples.label: Sentences (running example)
examples.purpose: A tiny natural-language grammar with long nonterminal names: no conflicts in any method.

examples.label: Arithmetic
examples.purpose: The expression grammar: LR(0) has conflicts that SLR(1) resolves.

examples.label: Arithmetic + parens
examples.purpose: Adds parentheses: nesting makes the automaton and the parse stack richer.

examples.label: Balanced parentheses
examples.purpose: Contains an ε-production: reductions that consume no input.

examples.label: Regular expressions
examples.purpose: Union, concatenation and postfix operators with left-recursive lists: no conflicts in SLR(1). Quoted terminals: '|' '*' '+' '?' '(' ')'.

examples.label: Shift-reduce
examples.purpose: A shift/reduce conflict: shift the next token or reduce first.

examples.label: Reduce-reduce
examples.purpose: A reduce/reduce conflict: two completed rules compete for the same input, id.

examples.label: Dangling else
examples.purpose: Conflict that survives even in LR(1), because the grammar is ambiguous.
text: S -> if E S else S

examples.label: LR(1) but not LALR(1)
examples.purpose: Merging LR(1) states with equal cores creates a reduce/reduce conflict that full LR(1) avoids.
text: // LR(1) but not LALR(1) — Aho, Sethi & Ullman
S -> a A d | b A e | a B e | b B d

examples.label: LALR(1) but not SLR(1)
examples.purpose: SLR(1)'s FOLLOW sets are too coarse here; LALR(1)'s precise lookaheads resolve the conflict.
text: // LALR(1) but not SLR(1) — Dragon Book classic
// SLR(1) conflict: = ∈ FOLLOW(R), so state with R→L•
// can't decide shift = vs reduce. LALR(1) resolves it
// because the lookahead for R→L• there is only $.

examples.label: SLR(1) but not LR(0)
examples.purpose: A reduce/reduce conflict in LR(0) that one symbol of lookahead (FOLLOW) resolves.

examples.label: LR(0) with extra LR(1) state
examples.purpose: The same grammar in LR(0) and LR(1): LR(1) splits a state by lookahead, so its automaton is larger.
text: // LR(0), but LR(1) has one extra state
S -> a A p | b A q

examples.label: Mini-Pascal
examples.purpose: A realistic grammar with dozens of states.
text: Stmt -> if Expr then Stmt else Stmt
Expr -> Expr + Term | Expr - Term | Term

examples.label: Pascal excerpt (declarations)
examples.purpose: Pascal declarations with left-recursive lists: LR(0) has conflicts that SLR(1) resolves. About a hundred states.
text: <proc> → procedure <phead_c> forward ; | procedure <phead_c> <block> ; | function <fhead_c> forward ; | function <fhead_c> <block> ;

examples.label: Right-recursive list (stack grows)
examples.purpose: Right recursion: the whole list sits on the stack before the first reduction.
text: // Compare with the left-recursive comma-separated list: here the stack holds the whole list

examples.label: Sentences with an adjective list (left-recursive)
examples.purpose: Left recursion in the adjective list, which LR parsers handle without rewriting.

examples.label: Even palindromes (not deterministic)
examples.purpose: No deterministic parser exists for this language: conflicts remain in every method.
text: // No LR(k) grammar exists: a PDA needs to guess the middle (see the PDA tool)
S -> a S a | b S b | eps
